JAMA Editors' Summary Podcast October 2, 2026
articles.abstract: Listen to the JAMA Editor’s Summary for an overview and discussion of the important articles appearing in JAMA.

articles.title: Societies Release Vaccine Recommendations for Respiratory Virus Season
articles.abstract: In the absence of updated federal guidance for the 2026 to 2027 respiratory virus season, US medical societies have published their own vaccine recommendations based on evidence reviews from the Vaccine Integrity Project, an initiative of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota. The up-to-date evidence reviews for influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) were published in JAMA.

articles.title: PREVENT Equations Integrated Into Electronic Health Record Platform
articles.abstract: The American Heart Association (AHA) announced that its PREVENT equations are now integrated into Epic’s electronic health record platform.

articles.title: Semaglutide Demonstrates Benefits Across Frailty Levels
articles.abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist semaglutide demonstrated safety and efficacy regardless of frailty status, a study published in JAMA Cardiology found.

articles.title: Autism Incidence Has Remained Stable, Study Finds
articles.abstract: The incidence of autism spectrum disorder in South Korea remained stable across cohorts born from 1998 to 2010, according to a study published in JAMA Pediatrics.

articles.title: CDC Issues Rabies Exposure Alert
articles.abstract: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a health advisory in response to reports of increased human exposure to rabid or possibly rabid animals.

articles.title: Addressing Cognitive Decline Among Aging Physicians
articles.abstract: Few explicit policies exist to address cognitive decline among aging physicians, a study published in JAMA Health Forum found.

articles.title: When Children Turn to AI Chatbots
articles.abstract: This Medical News article discusses how children are using artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for emotional support and the challenges of developing evidence and mental health safeguards quickly enough to keep pace with the technology.

articles.title: Can a Ketogenic Diet Improve Liver Health?
articles.abstract: This Medical News article discusses a randomized clinical trial that compared the metabolic effects of 10% weight loss with a Mediterranean diet, a very low-fat, plant-forward diet, and a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet.

articles.title: Blood Pressure Targets in Critically Ill Children
articles.abstract: “Do I need to treat this blood pressure?” is one of the most common questions to pass through the minds of acute care pediatricians during a typical day in the hospital. Blood pressure generally increases with somatic growth, reflecting developmental changes in stroke volume, vascular structure and function, and neurohumoral regulation. As a result of interindividual variation across the developmental stages of childhood, there is a wide range of acceptable blood pressure values. There is also long-standing ambiguity about what should be considered the limits of acceptable blood pressure, particularly among hospitalized children. Age-based reference values offer a starting point, although the threshold used to identify an unusually low blood pressure may differ from the pressure needed to maintain adequate organ perfusion. This uncertainty can create substantial tension when a clinician faces the decision whether to manage potentially low blood pressure in a child. Treatments for potentially low blood pressure can also vary widely, from temporary stimulation to administration of vasopressor and inotropic medications through a central vascular catheter. The clinical question of whether to manage low blood pressure is driven by concern that withholding treatment could cause harm that is hard to measure.

articles.title: Permissive Blood Pressure Targets in Pediatric Critical Care
articles.abstract: This randomized clinical trial examines whether adopting a permissive mean arterial blood pressure target improves outcomes in critically ill children with hypotension.

articles.title: Permissive Blood Pressure Targets in Pediatric Critical Care Research Summary
articles.abstract: This trial evaluated whether a permissive mean arterial pressure (MAP) target above the fifth percentile for age improves outcomes in hypotensive critically ill children.

articles.title: Father's Day
articles.abstract: A pediatrician writes about the barriers to appropriate pain relief she witnessed during her father’s last days in hospice.

articles.title: Prescription Drug Launch Price Trends Before and After the Inflation Reduction Act
articles.abstract: This study examines prescription drug launch prices over the last 2 decades and changes after the initiation of the Inflation Reduction Act.

articles.title: Licensure Framework for Autonomous Clinical Artificial Intelligence
articles.abstract: To the Editor The authors of a recent Perspective article proposed requiring autonomous clinical AI systems to score at or above the median of human test takers’ scores on the US Medical Licensing Examination and relevant specialty board examinations. The call for staged authorization is welcome, but this particular threshold asks written examinations to do something they were not designed to do: determine whether a system is ready to manage patients without per-case clinician review.

articles.title: Licensure Framework for Autonomous Clinical Artificial Intelligence
articles.abstract: To the Editor The authors of a recent Perspective article discussed a licensure framework for autonomous clinical AI systems making independent clinical determinations. Their proposal recognizes that autonomous AI requires clinical governance beyond conventional device clearance.

articles.title: Licensure Framework for Autonomous Clinical Artificial Intelligence
articles.abstract: To the Editor The proposed licensure framework for autonomous clinical AI in a recent Perspective is a thoughtful attempt to move beyond the static US Food and Drug Administration device-regulation model. However, 2 realities threaten the feasibility of treating AI as a licensed practitioner.

articles.title: Licensure Framework for Autonomous Clinical Artificial Intelligence
articles.abstract: To the Editor A recent Perspective proposed a federal licensure framework for autonomous clinical artificial intelligence (AI) modeled on physician credentialing. We disagree with the analogy. Medical licensure regulates a professional actor with fiduciary duties, moral agency, personal accountability, and the ability to refuse unsafe action. A software product has none of these. It is deployed by identifiable commercial and institutional actors. Granting it professional standing does not create accountability; it obscures it.

articles.title: Licensure Framework for Autonomous Clinical Artificial Intelligence—In Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank the correspondents for their Letters to the Editor, which converge on 1 concern—that autonomous clinical AI is not a person—and we agree. Our proposal never attributes moral agency to software, and licensure does not require it. Drs Ferguson and Telemi and Dr Jiang argue that a product cannot be a practitioner. But we do not license software as a moral actor; we authorize a defined clinical function and attach accountability to identifiable human parties. Developers bear primary responsibility and deploying institutions secondary responsibility precisely because the model cannot. Licensure here is a mechanism for ongoing, outcome-based authorization, not a claim of personhood.

articles.title: Errors in Confidence Intervals
articles.abstract: In the Original Investigation titled “Bivalent RSV Prefusion F Protein–Based Vaccine for Preventing Cardiovascular Hospitalizations in Older Adults: A Prespecified Analysis of the DAN-RSV Trial,” published in the October 28, 2025, issue of JAMA, a coding error caused incorrect calculation of the confidence intervals for vaccine effectiveness. These confidence intervals have been corrected in the Abstract, Results section of the text, Figure 2, Figure 3, Table 2, and Supplement 3. None of the corrected confidence intervals change the statistical interpretation of the results, no point estimates or P values are affected, and the overall conclusions of the study are unchanged. The accompanying Editorial has also been updated to reflect the changes. These articles were corrected online.

articles.title: AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support Tools
articles.abstract: To the Editor The Viewpoint article by Drs Singh and Mello provides a balanced discussion of advertising in artificial intelligence (AI)–powered clinical decision support (CDS). It is worth highlighting that the authors state that AI-powered CDS often is free. Did we not say the same about drug company–sponsored lunches and so-called “free” pens and other giveaways in the 1990s? Some will recall when drug companies sponsored lunches for faculty and trainees, gave away pens and other branded items, and sometimes accompanied physicians on rounds. For those who trained more recently, please know that this practice was widely accepted; however, we eventually learned that there is, in fact, no free lunch. Now, we must learn there is no free CDS. Singh and Mello note that while “some products operate on a subscription model, others such as OpenEvidence use advertising revenue to offer access without charge.” It is surprising and disappointing that clinicians may think they are receiving CDS for free. Perhaps they have forgotten—or may have never learned—that drug company advertisements influence prescribing behavior when they appear alongside information intended to educate physicians and support clinical practice. Clearly the drug companies themselves have not forgotten. Twenty years ago, the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations revised its code of ethics and barred gifts or money that could influence prescribing behavior. CDS companies that embed pharmaceutical advertisements in their products should end this practice and, if they do not, the pharmaceutical industry should do so. Better yet, clinicians should recognize they have other options without industry advertisements and should choose such CDS tools.

articles.title: AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support Tools
articles.abstract: To the Editor Drs Singh and Mello warn that advertising in AI-powered CDS tools offers unprecedented potential for industry to influence patient care. Additional risks arise when the AI technology itself is designed to advance commercial interests. However, bias must be avoided to prevent commercial interests, including pharmaceutical, device, and diagnostic testing companies, from affecting medical judgment and influencing prescribing.

articles.title: AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support Tools
articles.abstract: To the Editor Drs Singh and Mello rightly warn that advertising in AI-powered CDS tools could influence care at the point of clinical decisions. The most important guardrail should be a clinical query firewall. In AI-powered CDS, a query is not merely a search term. It may encode a provisional diagnosis, treatment uncertainty, molecular or imaging findings, medication history, comorbidity, or the clinician’s uncertainty about a specific patient. Turning that query into an advertising signal converts clinical reasoning into commercial inventory.

articles.title: AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support Tools—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We appreciate the thoughtful letters in response to our Viewpoint. We agree with Dr Ziegelstein that the simplest solution to the ethical quandaries of advertising in AI-powered CDS tools would be for the AI-powered CDS companies that use advertisements and/or the pharmaceutical companies that partner with them to end this practice altogether. However, this is unlikely to happen, given that advertising is a potentially more lucrative revenue source than other options such as subscriptions. Ziegelstein’s suggestion that clinicians recognize they have other options and choose CDS tools that do not embed advertisements seems more realistic, particularly if their organizational employers nudge them in this direction. Historically, once Epocrates (a free drug information app) began supporting ads at the point of care, its credibility with its physician users eroded and other services such as UpToDate ultimately won out.

articles.title: Intra-Arterial Tenecteplase After Endovascular Thrombectomy for Acute Stroke
articles.abstract: This secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial examines the efficacy of adjunctive intra-arterial tenecteplase 12 months after stroke in patients who received endovascular thrombectomy.

articles.title: Diagnostic Delays Associated With a Screening Trial of a Multicancer Early Detection Test
articles.abstract: To the Editor The article by Mr Mann and colleagues reported that regional participation in a population-based cell-free DNA–based multicancer early detection (MCED) trial was associated with a modest increase in diagnostic delay for patients referred for suspected head and neck, lung, and upper gastrointestinal cancers. The authors concluded that this delay is unlikely to materially influence the interpretation of trial results.

articles.title: Diagnostic Delays Associated With a Screening Trial of a Multicancer Early Detection Test—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We appreciate Dr Froehner’s thoughtful comments on our article reporting differentially higher diagnostic delay rates in regions participating in a population-based cell-free DNA–based MCED trial. As Dr Froehner notes, many health conditions are associated with poverty, as in the case of the lung, head and neck, and upper gastrointestinal cancers that we focused on in our study. Long-standing disparities in who receives preventive care, screening tests, and diagnostic follow-up contribute to these inequities.

articles.title: Will Women Physicians Face an AI Gap?
articles.abstract: Editor in Chief of JAMA+ AI Roy Perlis, MD, MSc, and Rochelle P. Walensky, MD, MPH, professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, discuss the role of women physicians in shaping AI’s impact on health care in this episode of the JAMA+ AI Conversations podcast.

articles.title: Errors in Results, Figure 3, and Supplement 1
articles.abstract: In the Original Investigation titled “Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography Scores to Predict Liver-Related Events in Steatotic Liver Disease,” published in the March 21, 2024, issue of JAMA, there were errors in the Results, Figure 3, and Supplement 1. In Results, the percentage given as 92.1% should have been 92.6%. In Supplement 1,the number 20.1 in eTable 10 should have been 20.6, the number 1.9 in eTable 17 should have been 11.9, the numbers 31.6 and 23.7 in eTable 18 should have been 3.6 and 237.7, respectively, and the headings “≥30% increase” and “<30% increase” in eTable 21 should have been reversed. In main article Figure 3, the listing “7, 0.01%” should have been “7, 0.1%.” This article was corrected online.

articles.title: The Physician of The Future
articles.abstract: In the midst of the present social upheaval, one may well wonder the position physicians will eventually occupy in the cosmic scheme. Intelligent observers inform us that the answer depends entirely on our own conduct—the mass conduct inherent in intelligent organization. If physicians are to assume that leadership essential to sane medical progress, they must evolve an outline of purposes, a constructive forward-looking program of things to be done, of channels through which cooperation must flow toward their leadership. This constructive program must be so wisely planned and so faithfully followed by all worth-while physicians that at least the intelligent element of public opinion will go with it.

articles.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Fecal Immunochemical Testing
articles.abstract: To the Editor The recent cost-effectiveness study by Dr Lee and colleagues provided important evidence supporting integrated gastric and colorectal cancer prevention through Helicobacter pylori stool antigen (HPSA) and fecal immunochemical test (FIT) co-testing. Co-testing with HPSA and FIT may offer a promising and economically attractive strategy in populations with high incidence of both gastric and colorectal cancers. Beyond demonstrating the potential value of this approach, the Taiwanese experience may also provide valuable lessons for countries seeking to strengthen cancer prevention programs.

articles.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Fecal Immunochemical Testing—Reply
articles.abstract: In Reply We thank Dr Huynh and colleagues for their thoughtful comments on our economic evaluation of HPSA-FIT co-testing. Rather than modeling a program developed de novo, we evaluated the incremental value of integrating HPSA testing into an established colorectal cancer screening program. Accordingly, infrastructure development costs were not included in our analysis; however, this should not be interpreted as suggesting implementation requires only minimal investment. Health system readiness varies considerably across countries, but we regard such heterogeneity as support for a staged implementation strategy rather than a limitation: countries with established FIT programs can readily add HPSA testing to existing stool-based testing pathways, whereas those with less mature systems may need to strengthen registries, laboratory networks, referral pathways, and treatment capacity.

articles.title: Holding Hope
articles.abstract: “What have you heard from the team?” I read the chart But I’m not asking what they said I wonder what you can hold

articles.title: Fixed Pupils: Neurologic Finality vs Poetic Repair
articles.abstract: In “Holding Hope,” the poem’s crux is not simply the devastating neurologic sign of “fixed pupils,” but also the way this medical phrase is transformed in the ear of the shocked sibling of a mortally wounded patient into the impossible mercy of healing: “[t]hey fixed his pupils.” The clinical distancing inherent in a bedside case presentation, reflexively performed before a disbelieving family member, is translated by a kind of poetic mishearing from incomprehensible loss into hopeful repair. The patient’s sibling seems to only grasp fragments of reality, while the physicians only offer partial truths. Even the clinician-speaker of the poem struggles with what can be held medically vs emotionally, the gasping lines and broken-up stanzas structurally reflecting the patient’s wounded brain and body and the heartbreak of both family member and physician. Yet poetry here does not really restore hope like some kind of harmless magic bullet, nor does it heal the lethal real-world gunshot wounds; more painfully, perhaps, it tries to reconcile brutal finality with the disconsolate wish it were not so. Thus the poem ultimately becomes an “antipresentation” of sorts, in which medical facts are melded with human truths, words can have double meanings, and what can be held is both the obligatory, dire prognosis and its denial. The insistence on what poetry can hear, and what no case presentation could ever convey, is reiterated in the poem’s final lines, expressed in the importunate paradox of the patient’s sibling’s repeated words: “…you heard/‘They fixed his pupils.’”

articles.title: Rural Emergency Hospitals
articles.abstract: This Perspective discusses the Rural Emergency Hospital designation, outlining structural flaws in its design and offering suggestions on how to address those flaws to encourage wider adoption.

articles.title: Protecting Patients From Politicization of Federal Science
articles.abstract: This Perspective discusses new proposed federal rules regarding research funding; the ways these rules could affect patients, communities, and taxpayers; and how federally supported research has benefitted public health.

articles.title: Review of Vaccines for Cancer
articles.abstract: This translational science review examines antigen-based cancer vaccines, which help patients develop immunity to the cellular protein expressed by cancer by stimulating the adaptive immune system.

articles.title: Intrauterine Mepivacaine Instillation vs Placebo for Pain During IUD Placement
articles.abstract: This randomized clinical trial assesses whether intrauterine instillation of mepivacaine reduces pain and improved tolerability during intrauterine device placement in nulliparous individuals.

articles.title: Intrauterine Mepivacaine Instillation vs Placebo for Pain During IUD Placement Research Summary
articles.abstract: This trial tested whether intrauterine mepivacaine reduces pain during intrauterine device (IUD) placement in nulliparous individuals.

articles.title: Asymptomatic Carotid Revascularization May Be Justified, but Not to Improve Cognition
articles.abstract: Stroke is a feared complication of atherosclerotic carotid artery stenosis. After years of debate regarding the value of revascularizing asymptomatic carotid stenosis in the modern era of intensive medical prevention with antiplatelet therapy and high-intensity statins, the CREST-2 trial revisited this question in a pair of randomized clinical trials: one trial comparing carotid endarterectomy plus best medical management vs medical therapy alone and the other comparing carotid artery stenting plus best medical management vs medial therapy alone. The topline findings showed that carotid artery stenting, but not carotid endarterectomy, significantly reduced the risk of the primary outcome of a composite of stroke or death within 44 days or ipsilateral stroke within up to 4 years compared with medical therapy alone among patients without contralateral stenosis who were good procedural candidates.

articles.title: Revascularization in Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis With Hemodynamic Impairment
articles.abstract: This substudy of a randomized clinical trial examines whether carotid artery revascularization with carotid stenting or endarterectomy improves cognitive outcomes differentially depending on whether there is impaired cerebral hemodynamic flow at baseline.

articles.title: Cognitive Outcomes After Revascularization of Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis
articles.abstract: This report from the Carotid Revascularization and Medical Management for Asymptomatic Carotid Stenosis Trials (CREST-2) describes the effects of carotid revascularization on cognitive outcomes in CREST-2 participants.

articles.title: Revascularization in Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis With Hemodynamic Impairment and Cognitive Outcomes Research Summary
articles.abstract: This study tested whether cognitive benefit from revascularization in asymptomatic high-grade internal carotid artery stenosis varied by baseline cerebral hemodynamic impairment.

articles.title: Patient Information: Hip Fracture
articles.abstract: This JAMA Patient Page describes how common a hip fracture is, risk factors, how it is diagnosed and treated, and the prognosis.

articles.title: Medications for Alcohol Use Disorder
articles.abstract: This JAMA Insights examines US Food and Drug Administration–approved medications for alcohol use disorder, including the dosing, efficacy, and adverse effects of naltrexone, acamprosate, and disulfiram.

articles.title: From Breakthrough to Follow-Through—A Public Health Agenda for AI
articles.abstract: This Viewpoint discusses the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in ensuring that patients eligible for highly effective interventions are identified and receive them.
